transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doc, what brings me in is... I just keep forgetting things I really shouldn't be forgetting. Like, uh, my heart follow-up appointments. I missed the last one, and the receptionist over there—she's a real piece of work, always got this scowl on her face, and they have those awful vinyl chairs in the waiting room that just stick to your pants. But anyway, I keep forgetting to call the clinic back. 

And it's not just the medical stuff, either. The other day I went over to help my neighbor fix his fence—he’s got this golden retriever that keeps digging under the wooden posts, beautiful dog, really, but a total menace to the landscaping—and I get all the way out to his yard and realize I showed up without the right tools for the repair job. Left my whole belt sitting on the workbench in my garage. I mean, who drives all the way over to do a job and forgets the tools? So, yeah, my wife said I needed to come talk to somebody about it.
When did you first start noticing these memory problems? Was it something that came on suddenly over days or weeks, or has this been going on for months or years?

Well, let's see... it definitely wasn't overnight. I'd say it's been causing real trouble for about a year and two months now. It all started right around the time I had this cardiac scare. Scared the living daylights out of my wife, I tell ya. 

Because of that whole ordeal, the doctors forced me to cut back on all my walking and the heavy garage projects that used to keep me settled. I used to walk three miles every single morning, right down past the old elementary school—they just painted the outside of it this awful shade of yellow, by the way. It looks like a giant mustard bottle just sitting at the end of the street. I have no idea who approved that at the town meeting, probably the same guy who thought we needed a third traffic light on Main Street. 

But anyway, yeah, since I had to stop moving around so much and tinkering with my projects, I just can't seem to keep my head screwed on straight.

Besides the forgotten appointments and tools, have other people who know you well—like your wife or close friends—noticed that your memory or thinking seems off, or is it mainly something you've noticed yourself?

Oh, they’ve definitely noticed. My wife, for one, she never lets me hear the end of it. But it's not just her, it's the guys down at the senior center, too. I volunteer with this repair group there—we fix up old lamps, wobbly chairs, that sort of thing for folks in the neighborhood. We used to get a lot of old radios, actually, but nobody keeps those anymore. It's a real shame, honestly, because the craftsmanship on those old wooden casings was just beautiful. You don't see dovetail joints like that on anything you buy at the big box stores today. Now it's all just cheap particle board that crumbles if it gets even a little bit damp. I bought a bookshelf for my grandson last year and I swear half the screws stripped before they even went in... 

But anyway, what was I... oh, right, the memory thing. Yeah, the guys at the center, it's gotten to where they can't really count on me the way they used to. I'll say I'm coming in on a Tuesday to fix a toaster and just completely blank on it. And like I mentioned earlier, my doctor’s office has had to literally chase me down about those missed heart follow-ups. They call the house constantly. Usually I don't even want to answer the landline anymore because of all those scam calls you get nowadays. You know, the ones where a robot tells you your car warranty is expiring? I haven't owned a car with a warranty since 1998! I drive a '95 Ford, runs like a top if you treat her right. But yeah, to answer your question, other people are definitely seeing it. It's not just in my head.
Besides the heart scare you mentioned, have you ever had a stroke, a TIA—that's a mini-stroke—or any problems with high blood pressure or diabetes?

No, no, nothing like that. No strokes or mini-strokes, thank God. And my blood pressure is actually pretty good for a guy my age, and no diabetes either. I try to eat right, you know? My wife makes sure of it. She’s got me on this low-sodium kick ever since the heart thing. We don't even buy regular salt anymore, just that pink Himalayan stuff. I don't know if it actually does anything different, but she swears by it. She read this article in one of those magazines she gets—the ones with the recipes that take three hours to make and use ingredients you can't even find at the regular grocery store. I had to drive all the way two towns over just to find some specific kind of vinegar she wanted last week. The traffic was unbelievable, too. They’ve got the highway down to one lane for construction, and they’ve been working on that same stretch of road for what feels like five years. You'd think with all the taxes we pay, they could fix a pothole in under a decade, but no. I was sitting there idling for twenty minutes just watching this guy in a hard hat lean on a shovel... but anyway, no, no strokes or diabetes or anything like that. Just the heart scare.

You mentioned these memory problems started about a year and two months ago after your heart scare. Do your memory and thinking problems stay pretty much the same from day to day, or do they get noticeably better or worse at different times?

You know, I haven't really paid attention to whether it's worse on some days than others. Honestly, since I retired, the days just kind of blend together anyway. It's hard to keep track of what day it even is unless it's a Tuesday, because that's trash day. 

And let me tell you, the city just switched over to those new automated garbage trucks a few months ago, right? So they gave everybody on the block these massive green bins. They're heavy, they're incredibly awkward to drag down the driveway, and half the time the mechanical arm on the truck knocks the lid completely off into the street anyway! I had to go out there in my slippers last week just to chase my lid down before the wind blew it into Mrs. Gable's yard. She’s already mad at me because my big oak tree drops acorns on her driveway, which, frankly, is just what trees do. You can't control nature. I told her, I said, "Martha, if I could tell the tree where to drop 'em, I would." But she just scowled at me. She's had a chip on her shoulder ever since her cat ran away in 2019. 

But anyway... what were we talking about? Oh, if my memory changes from day to day. Yeah, I really couldn't tell you. I haven't noticed any kind of pattern to it. It just feels like I'm always kind of scattered lately, no matter what day it is.

Looking back over this past year and two months since your heart scare, would you say your memory and thinking problems have been getting gradually worse, staying about the same, or have they actually improved at all?

Getting worse... you know, a year and two months, that puts the heart thing right around Halloween, I think? Yeah, because we had just bought those massive bags of candy from Costco. My wife always insists on buying the name-brand chocolate because she doesn't want us to be "that house" on the block. You know the ones, they hand out those weird little peanut butter taffy things wrapped in the plain orange and black paper? Nobody even likes those! I swear they just recycle the same batch from 1975 every year. 

I actually broke a crown on one of those back when I was still working at the plant. Had to go to Dr. Miller—terrible dentist, by the way, real heavy hands. He retired a few years ago and moved down to Florida. Boca, I think. Or maybe Sarasota. I don't know how anybody stands the humidity down there, honestly. My brother-in-law went down there for a golf trip last summer and came back with a sunburn so bad he couldn't put a real shirt on for three days. He was walking around the house in this shiny silk robe looking like Hugh Hefner, it was ridiculous... 

But, wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, if the memory is getting worse. Honestly, Doc, I really couldn't tell you. I haven't kept track of it like that. It's just bad. I don't know if it's a worse bad or the exact same bad as it was last year, to be honest with you.
Besides forgetting things, have you noticed any problems finding the right words when you're talking, or do you ever feel confused about where you are or what time of day it is?

Finding the right words? No, no, I don't think so. I mean, I talk plenty, you can probably tell that. My wife says I could talk the ear off a brass monkey. She actually bought one of those monkeys once, at a flea market up near the lake. We used to go up there every summer, rent this little cabin. It didn't have AC, just these flimsy screen doors that let all the mosquitoes in. I spent half the vacation swatting at bugs with a rolled-up newspaper. You know, they don't even print the local paper every day anymore? It's just Wednesdays and Sundays now. It's a shame, I used to like doing the crossword puzzle with my morning coffee. Now I just look out the window at Mrs. Gable's yard. 

But no, I don't get confused about where I am or anything like that. I know I'm right here in the clinic, and it's... well, it's daytime. I don't know the exact time, I don't wear a watch anymore since the battery died on my Timex. I took it to the jeweler in the mall to get it fixed, but the whole mall is practically empty now. Half the stores are boarded up. It's depressing, really. Used to be the place to go on a Saturday afternoon. But yeah, no problems with words or knowing where I am. Just the memory stuff.

When you had that cardiac scare about a year ago, did you lose consciousness at any point, or did you pass out? And did the doctors tell you that your heart stopped or that you weren't getting enough oxygen to your brain?

Lose consciousness? Pass out? No, I don't think so. I mean, I remember the whole thing pretty clearly. Well, as clearly as you can remember being strapped to a stretcher while a bunch of paramedics are shouting at each other. They were making such a racket, you'd think they were trying to wake the dead. And the siren! Good grief, they had that thing blaring the whole way to the hospital, and we only live about two miles away. 

I kept trying to tell the guy in the back with me—young kid, couldn't have been a day over twenty, barely had a mustache—I said, "Son, you don't need the siren, there's no traffic on Elm Street at 10 AM on a Thursday." But he just ignored me and kept checking my blood pressure. They always pump those cuffs up way too tight, don't they? It feels like they're trying to pop your arm right off. I had a bruise shaped like a crescent moon for a week after that. My wife told me to put some arnica cream on it, she swears by that stuff. Buys it in these little yellow tubes from the health food store downtown. The one next to the old movie theater? They turned the theater into a rock climbing gym, if you can believe that. People paying good money to hang off plastic rocks indoors when there's a whole mountain range two hours away. Makes no sense to me. 

But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, the heart thing. No, nobody ever said my heart stopped or anything about oxygen to the brain. Just a scare, they called it. Kept me overnight, ran a bunch of tests, gave me a breakfast tray the next morning with the saddest-looking scrambled eggs I've ever seen in my life. Looked like yellow sponge. I didn't eat 'em.

When you were at the hospital after that cardiac scare, did the doctors ever mention anything about your heart rhythm being abnormal, or did they say anything about your heart stopping or going into a dangerous rhythm like ventricular fibrillation?

Abnormal rhythm? No, no, they didn't say anything like that. No stopping, no... whatever that other word you just said was. Ventricular something. It just felt like my chest was doing a washing machine cycle, honestly. But the doctors didn't say it was a dangerous rhythm or anything. 

Speaking of washing machines, we had to replace ours right after I got out of the hospital. The old Maytag finally gave up the ghost. Sounded like a jet engine taking off in the basement every time it hit the spin cycle. My wife made me go to Sears to look at new ones, but Sears is closed now, isn't it? We ended up at Home Depot. The guy there—wearing an orange apron, name tag said 'Kevin'—tried to sell us one of those smart washers that connects to the Wi-Fi. I said, "Kevin, why on earth does my washing machine need the internet? Is it going to email me when the socks are clean?" It's ridiculous. Everything has to have a computer in it now. Even my toaster has a digital screen. It's a toaster! You push the lever down, the bread gets hot. You don't need a microchip for that. 

But anyway, no, they didn't say my heart stopped or went into a crazy rhythm. Just a scare, like I said.

When you had that cardiac scare, did the doctors ever tell you that your heart completely stopped beating, or that you weren't getting enough oxygen and your brain wasn't getting blood flow for a period of time?

No, they never said anything like that. They didn't say it stopped completely, and nobody mentioned anything about my brain not getting blood or oxygen or whatever. I think I would've remembered if they told me my brain wasn't getting blood. That sounds pretty serious. 

But you know, speaking of blood, they drew so much of it while I was in there. It felt like they were trying to drain me dry. This one nurse, she came in at three in the morning—three in the morning!—just to take more blood. She had this little cart that squeaked every time the wheels turned. Squeak, squeak, squeak, all the way down the hall. You'd think a hospital would have some WD-40 lying around. I keep a can of it in the garage, right next to my fishing tackle. I haven't been fishing in ages, though. The lake's gotten so crowded lately, all these speedboats zipping around, scaring the bass away. You can't even enjoy a quiet morning out on the water anymore without some guy on a jet ski doing donuts fifty feet from your boat. 

But yeah, no, my heart didn't stop, and my brain was getting plenty of oxygen as far as I know. Just... just that washing machine feeling in my chest.

I want to make sure I understand the heart event clearly. When you were having that chest problem and they brought you to the hospital, did you ever lose consciousness or black out at any point—even for just a few seconds—before, during, or right after the ambulance ride?

No, no, I never blacked out or lost consciousness or anything like that. Not even for a second. I was wide awake the whole time, watching the whole circus happen. Like I said, I remember the ambulance ride, I remember the squeaky cart, all of it. 

I actually remember looking out the back window of the ambulance and seeing Mrs. Gable's house as we went past. She lives on the corner of Elm and Maple. She's got these huge hydrangeas in her front yard, beautiful blue ones. She told my wife her secret is putting coffee grounds in the soil to make it acidic. We tried it last spring, saved all our Folgers grounds in a plastic tub under the sink. But our dog, Buster—he's a beagle mix, nose gets him into all sorts of trouble—he got into the tub and ate half the coffee grounds. I had to call the emergency vet at ten o'clock at night. Cost me two hundred dollars just for them to tell me he was gonna be jittery for a day and to make sure he drank water. He was practically vibrating, running laps around the coffee table until 3 AM. 

But no, I didn't pass out or black out at all with the heart thing. I was awake for the whole ordeal.

When you had that cardiac scare and went to the hospital, did the doctors ever tell you that your heart had stopped beating or that you had gone into cardiac arrest—where your heart completely quit working for a while?

Doc, I feel like we're going in circles a bit here! No, they never said cardiac arrest. It didn't stop beating, and it definitely didn't quit working. If my heart completely quit working, I'm pretty sure I wouldn't be sitting in this chair talking to you right now. 

But you know, hearing the word arrest... it reminds me, my nephew Tommy almost got arrested last week. Well, not arrested, just a speeding ticket, but the boy acted like he was headed for the state pen. Got pulled over on Route 9 doing sixty in a forty-five zone. It was a state trooper, too. You know the ones with those wide-brimmed hats? They do not mess around. Tommy actually tried to tell the guy his speedometer was broken. I said, Tommy, you don't tell a cop your car is broken, they'll just write you another ticket for that! Kids these days, they think they can talk their way out of anything. 

Back when I was his age, if you got caught speeding, the cop would just follow you home and tell your dad. And let me tell you, my dad finding out was way worse than paying a fine to the city. He made me paint our entire garage, inside and out, in the middle of July. Took me three whole weekends, and I got paint in my hair that wouldn't wash out for a month. Looked like I had a weird gray stripe right down the middle of my head. 

But anyway, to answer your question again, no. No cardiac arrest, the heart never stopped beating. Just that crazy fluttering feeling.
When you had that cardiac event, was there any time—even a minute or two—where you don't remember what happened, or where other people had to tell you what occurred because you weren't aware of it?

No, no lost time at all. I remember every single second of it, loud and clear. Nobody had to fill me in on anything because I was right there for the whole show. 

You know, speaking of not remembering things, my wife's been complaining about her memory lately. She says she walks into a room and completely forgets why she went in there. I told her, "Honey, that's just getting older." But she's convinced it's because of this new diet she's on. She read somewhere that cutting out all carbs makes your brain foggy for the first couple of weeks. Keto, I think they call it? She's got me eating cauliflower mashed potatoes now. Let me tell you, you can mash a cauliflower all you want, you can drown it in butter and garlic, but it is never, ever going to taste like a real potato. It's just mushy disappointment. I tried to sneak a real potato into the grocery cart last week, just one little Russet, but she caught me in the produce aisle. Gave me that look she gets, you know the one. 

But yeah, anyway, my memory of the whole hospital trip is perfectly fine. Didn't miss a beat. Well, I mean, my heart missed a beat, or added a few, but my brain was perfectly aware the whole time.

After you got to the hospital and they were examining you, did any of the doctors or nurses ever tell you that you had stopped breathing, or that you needed oxygen through a mask or tube to help you breathe?

No, nobody said anything about me stopping breathing. I didn't need a tube or anything like that. They might have put those little prongs in my nose for a minute, you know, the plastic ones, but I was breathing on my own just fine. 

Although, you know who does stop breathing? My brother-in-law, Gary. He's got that sleep apnea thing. Have you ever heard someone with sleep apnea? It is terrifying. My wife and I went on a cruise with Gary and my sister a couple years ago—one of those Alaskan cruises, beautiful scenery, highly recommend it if you don't mind the cold. We saw a glacier calve, just massive chunks of ice falling into the water. Sounded like a cannon going off. But anyway, we had adjoining cabins, and the walls on those ships are paper thin. I swear to you, I would lie awake at night listening to Gary snore like a freight train, and then suddenly... dead silence. Just nothing. I'd sit up in bed waiting for the guy to take a breath, thinking I was gonna have to bust through the door and do CPR. Then, out of nowhere, he'd make this loud snorting, choking noise and start the whole cycle over again. My sister sleeps right through it! I don't know how she does it. She says she bought him one of those CPAP machines, the ones that look like a fighter pilot mask, but he refuses to wear it because it messes up his hair. The guy is sixty-five and going bald, I don't know what hair he thinks he's protecting. 

But no, I didn't stop breathing during the heart thing. I was panting a little bit because I was scared, sure, but I didn't stop.

During that moment when you were having the chest problem—right when it was happening, before the ambulance even arrived—did you ever feel like you were losing consciousness, or did everything go black or fuzzy for even just a moment or two?

No, no, I never felt like I was passing out or anything. Everything was clear, just... scary, you know? No blacking out, no fuzziness. 

Speaking of fuzzy, though, you should see the new rug my daughter just bought for her living room. It's one of those shag carpets, but like, extreme shag. I don't know what the style is called, but it looks like a giant, flat sheep dog just sleeping in the middle of the floor. I told her, I said, "Sarah, how are you ever going to vacuum that thing?" You drop a peanut in there, it's gone forever. It's just part of the ecosystem now. And she's got a golden retriever! That dog sheds enough to build a whole second dog every week. I give it a month before that rug is just a solid mat of dog hair and crumbs. 

I remember when my wife and I bought our first house, we had this beautiful hardwood floor, but she insisted we cover it up with wall-to-wall carpeting. It was the style back then, I guess. Forest green. The whole downstairs looked like a golf course. We spent a fortune on it, and then ten years later, what do we do? We rip it all up because hardwood was back in style! We spent a whole weekend pulling up staples. My knees haven't been the same since. 

But no, to answer your question, my head was perfectly clear during the chest thing. Just a lot of panic, but no passing out.

When you were in the hospital after that heart scare, did the doctors ever show you any records or tell you that your heart had actually stopped beating for any amount of time, or that your heart went into a rhythm where it wasn't pumping blood properly to your body?

No, they never said anything like that. They hooked me up to all those monitors, and they were beeping away, but nobody ever said my heart actually stopped or wasn't pumping right. 

You know, speaking of things not pumping right, my sump pump in the basement has been giving me absolute fits lately. We had that big storm roll through last Tuesday—did you get any of that rain where you live? It came down in buckets. I was down there in my slippers at two in the morning, watching the water creep up toward my workbench. I have all my power tools down there, my table saw, my drill press. If that water had gotten another two inches higher, it would have ruined thousands of dollars of equipment. I bought this pump, top of the line, supposed to handle anything, but the float switch keeps getting stuck. I keep telling my son he needs to come over and help me dig out the pit, make it a little wider, but you know kids these days. He's always "busy with work" or "taking the kids to soccer." When I was his age, if my dad called and said he needed help, I dropped what I was doing and I went. Different generation, I guess. We ended up bailing water with a five-gallon bucket for three hours. My shoulder is still barking at me from that. 

But anyway, yeah, the doctors never mentioned my heart stopping. Just said it was a scare, you know? Kept me for observation, but no stopping.
During that cardiac scare or right after it happened, did you ever have any seizures, convulsions, or jerking movements of your arms or legs—even if just for a few seconds?

No, nothing like that. No seizures or jerking around. I was perfectly still. Well, as still as you can be when you're strapped to a stretcher, anyway, but no, my body wasn't doing anything weird. 

Although, you know what does jerk around like crazy? Our washing machine. My wife overloaded it with heavy bath towels just the other day. I keep telling her, you can't just throw all the heavy stuff in on one side of the agitator, it throws the whole drum out of whack. It got to the spin cycle and sounded like a helicopter was landing in our laundry room. Bang, bang, bang! The whole machine actually walked itself about three inches across the linoleum. I had to get back there with a pry bar just to shimmy the darn thing back into place. 

They really don't make appliances like they used to, do they? My mother had this old Maytag when I was growing up, thing must have lasted thirty years. Thirty years! Now you buy a machine, it's got a computer board in it, it connects to the Wi-Fi... why on earth does a washing machine need Wi-Fi? Is it going to send me an email when my socks are clean? It's just more parts that can break, if you ask me. You pay a thousand dollars for a machine and you're lucky if it lasts five years before the motherboard fries. 

But anyway, no, no convulsions or shaking for me. Just my poor washing machine.

I know you've said you didn't black out, but I want to be very specific: when you were having that chest problem, did anyone—the paramedics, the ER doctors, your wife—ever tell you that you were unresponsive or that they couldn't wake you up or get you to respond to them, even if you don't remember it yourself?

No, no one ever said anything like that. My wife was right there the whole time, and the paramedics were talking to me all the way to the hospital. I was answering their questions, giving them my name and date of birth, all that stuff. So no, I was never unresponsive. 

Speaking of unresponsive, though, you should try getting a straight answer out of the cable company these days. I spent two hours on the phone with them yesterday. Two hours! My bill went up by thirty dollars this month, no warning, nothing. Just boom, thirty more dollars. So I call them up, and first you have to talk to that robot lady. "Press one for billing, press two for technical support." I just start pressing zero, trying to get a real human being. Finally, I get this guy—I think his name was Kevin—and I say, "Kevin, why is my bill thirty dollars higher?" And he starts giving me this runaround about promotional periods ending and regional sports fees. I don't even watch sports! I watch the History Channel and those shows where they build log cabins in Alaska. Why am I paying for a regional sports fee? 

I told Kevin, I said, "Look, I've been a customer for fifteen years. You're going to put my bill back to what it was, or I'm switching to that satellite dish." He puts me on hold for twenty minutes, comes back, and says the best he can do is a five-dollar credit. Five dollars! It's highway robbery, is what it is. I remember when we first got cable back in the eighties, it was twenty bucks a month and you got every channel under the sun. Now you pay an arm and a leg just to watch commercials. 

But no, nobody said I was unresponsive during the chest thing. I was awake and talking the whole time.

I want to go back to the hospital records from that cardiac event one more time. Did the doctors give you any paperwork or discharge summary that mentioned your heart stopping, or did they ever use the term 'cardiac arrest' or 'code blue' in any of the paperwork they sent home with you?

No, I read through all those discharge papers when I got home. My wife keeps everything in this big accordion folder, very organized. There was nothing in there about cardiac arrest or a code blue or anything like that. Just some stuff about a minor arrhythmia and keeping an eye on my cholesterol. 

You know, speaking of paperwork, the amount of junk mail we get these days is just out of control. I go out to the mailbox every afternoon, and it's just stuffed full of credit card offers, catalogs for things I'd never buy in a million years, and those glossy flyers for real estate agents. "We can sell your house for top dollar!" I'm not selling my house! We've lived there for thirty-five years. I planted the oak tree in the front yard myself when it was just a sapling. Now it shades the whole driveway. But every day, it's a stack of paper this thick, straight from the mailbox into the recycling bin. It's a terrible waste of trees, if you ask me. I tried calling one of those numbers once to get off their mailing list, but it was just an automated system that hung up on me. 

But yeah, no, the hospital paperwork didn't say anything about my heart stopping.

I know this might sound like an odd question, but sometimes when people have a serious heart problem, their family members notice things they themselves don't remember. Did your wife ever tell you that during that cardiac scare, you stopped responding to her, or that she was trying to talk to you and you weren't answering her—even if you have no memory of that happening?

No, my wife never said anything like that. She was right there, holding my hand, and I was talking to her the whole time. I was scared, sure, but I never stopped answering her. 

You know, she's always been a talker, my wife. We've been married forty-two years, and I swear she hasn't stopped talking since the day we met at the county fair. She was wearing this yellow sundress... or was it blue? No, it was yellow, because she spilled mustard on it from a corn dog. Anyway, she can talk to anybody. We go to the grocery store, and she's chatting up the cashier about their grandchildren, the bag boy about his college classes... a ten-minute trip for milk turns into a forty-five-minute social event. I usually just wander over to the hardware aisle and look at the lightbulbs. Did you know they barely sell regular incandescent bulbs anymore? It's all those LED ones now. They cost an arm and a leg, and the light they give off is so... sterile, you know? Like a hospital room. I miss the warm glow of the old bulbs. I actually bought a whole case of them at a garage sale a few years back, just to have them on hand. 

But no, to answer your question, she never said I stopped responding to her. I was awake and talking the whole time.

Oh, they’ve definitely noticed. My wife, for one, she never lets me hear the end of it. But it's not just her, it's the guys down at the senior center, too. I volunteer with this repair group there—we fix up old lamps, wobbly chairs, that sort of thing for folks in the neighborhood. We used to get a lot of old radios, actually, but nobody keeps those anymore. It's a real shame, honestly, because the craftsmanship on those old wooden casings was just beautiful. You don't see dovetail joints like that on anything you buy at the big box stores today. Now it's all just cheap particle board that crumbles if it gets even a little bit damp. I bought a bookshelf for my grandson last year and I swear half the screws stripped before they even went in... 

But anyway, what was I... oh, right, the memory thing. Yeah, the guys at the center, it's gotten to where they can't really count on me the way they used to. I'll say I'm coming in on a Tuesday to fix a toaster and just completely blank on it. And like I mentioned earlier, my doctor’s office has had to literally chase me down about those missed heart follow-ups. They call the house constantly. Usually I don't even want to answer the landline anymore because of all those scam calls you get nowadays. You know, the ones where a robot tells you your car warranty is expiring? I haven't owned a car with a warranty since 1998! I drive a '95 Ford, runs like a top if you treat her right. But yeah, to answer your question, other people are definitely seeing it. I don't know if it actually does anything different, but she swears by it. She read this article in one of those magazines she gets—the ones with the recipes that take three hours to make and use ingredients you can't even find at the regular grocery store. They’ve got the highway down to one lane for construction, and they’ve been working on that same stretch of road for what feels like five years. And let me tell you, the city just switched over to those new automated garbage trucks a few months ago, right? So they gave everybody on the block these massive green bins. They're heavy, they're incredibly awkward to drag down the driveway, and half the time the mechanical arm on the truck knocks the lid completely off into the street anyway! I had to go out there in my slippers last week just to chase my lid down before the wind blew it into Mrs. Gable's yard. She’s already mad at me because my big oak tree drops acorns on her driveway, which, frankly, is just what trees do. You can't control nature. I told her, I said, "Martha, if I could tell the tree where to drop 'em, I would." But she just scowled at me. She's had a chip on her shoulder ever since her cat ran away in 2019. 

But anyway... what were we talking about? Oh, if my memory changes from day to day. Yeah, I really couldn't tell you. I haven't noticed any kind of pattern to it. It just feels like I'm always kind of scattered lately, no matter what day it is.

You know the ones, they hand out those weird little peanut butter taffy things wrapped in the plain orange and black paper? Nobody even likes those! I swear they just recycle the same batch from 1975 every year. 

I actually broke a crown on one of those back when I was still working at the plant. Had to go to Dr. Miller—terrible dentist, by the way, real heavy hands. He retired a few years ago and moved down to Florida. Boca, I think. Or maybe Sarasota. I don't know how anybody stands the humidity down there, honestly. My brother-in-law went down there for a golf trip last summer and came back with a sunburn so bad he couldn't put a real shirt on for three days. He was walking around the house in this shiny silk robe looking like Hugh Hefner, it was ridiculous... 

But, wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, if the memory is getting worse. Honestly, Doc, I really couldn't tell you. I haven't kept track of it like that. It's just bad. I don't know if it's a worse bad or the exact same bad as it was last year, to be honest with you.

You know, they don't even print the local paper every day anymore? It's just Wednesdays and Sundays now. It's a shame, I used to like doing the crossword puzzle with my morning coffee. Now I just look out the window at Mrs. Gable's yard. 

But no, I don't get confused about where I am or anything like that. I know I'm right here in the clinic, and it's... well, it's daytime. I don't know the exact time, I don't wear a watch anymore since the battery died on my Timex. I took it to the jeweler in the mall to get it fixed, but the whole mall is practically empty now. Half the stores are boarded up. It's depressing, really. Used to be the place to go on a Saturday afternoon. But yeah, no problems with words or knowing where I am. Just the memory stuff.

patient.answer:
Lose consciousness? Pass out? No, I don't think so. I mean, I remember the whole thing pretty clearly. Well, as clearly as you can remember being strapped to a stretcher while a bunch of paramedics are shouting at each other. They were making such a racket, you'd think they were trying to wake the dead. And the siren! Good grief, they had that thing blaring the whole way to the hospital, and we only live about two miles away. 

I kept trying to tell the guy in the back with me—young kid, couldn't have been a day over twenty, barely had a mustache—I said, "Son, you don't need the siren, there's no traffic on Elm Street at 10 AM on a Thursday." But he just ignored me and kept checking my blood pressure. They always pump those cuffs up way too tight, don't they? It feels like they're trying to pop your arm right off. I had a bruise shaped like a crescent moon for a week after that. My wife told me to put some arnica cream on it, she swears by that stuff. Buys it in these little yellow tubes from the health food store downtown. The one next to the old movie theater? They turned the theater into a rock climbing gym, if you can believe that. People paying good money to hang off plastic rocks indoors when there's a whole mountain range two hours away. Makes no sense to me. 

But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, the heart thing. No, nobody ever said my heart stopped or anything about oxygen to the brain. Just a scare, they called it. Kept me overnight, ran a bunch of tests, gave me a breakfast tray the next morning with the saddest-looking scrambled eggs I've ever seen in my life. Looked like yellow sponge. I didn't eat 'em.

Speaking of washing machines, we had to replace ours right after I got out of the hospital. The old Maytag finally gave up the ghost. Sounded like a jet engine taking off in the basement every time it hit the spin cycle. My wife made me go to Sears to look at new ones, but Sears is closed now, isn't it? We ended up at Home Depot. The guy there—wearing an orange apron, name tag said 'Kevin'—tried to sell us one of those smart washers that connects to the Wi-Fi. I said, "Kevin, why on earth does my washing machine need the internet? Is it going to email me when the socks are clean?" It's ridiculous. Everything has to have a computer in it now. Even my toaster has a digital screen. It's a toaster! You push the lever down, the bread gets hot. You don't need a microchip for that. 

But anyway, no, they didn't say my heart stopped or went into a crazy rhythm. Just a scare, like I said.

No, they never said anything like that. They didn't say it stopped completely, and nobody mentioned anything about my brain not getting blood or oxygen or whatever. I think I would've remembered if they told me my brain wasn't getting blood. That sounds pretty serious.

This one nurse, she came in at three in the morning—three in the morning!—just to take more blood. She had this little cart that squeaked every time the wheels turned. Squeak, squeak, squeak, all the way down the hall. You'd think a hospital would have some WD-40 lying around. I keep a can of it in the garage, right next to my fishing tackle. I haven't been fishing in ages, though. The lake's gotten so crowded lately, all these speedboats zipping around, scaring the bass away. You can't even enjoy a quiet morning out on the water anymore without some guy on a jet ski doing donuts fifty feet from your boat. 

But yeah, no, my heart didn't stop, and my brain was getting plenty of oxygen as far as I know. Just... just that washing machine feeling in my chest.

I actually remember looking out the back window of the ambulance and seeing Mrs. Gable's house as we went past. She lives on the corner of Elm and Maple. She's got these huge hydrangeas in her front yard, beautiful blue ones. She told my wife her secret is putting coffee grounds in the soil to make it acidic. We tried it last spring, saved all our Folgers grounds in a plastic tub under the sink. But our dog, Buster—he's a beagle mix, nose gets him into all sorts of trouble—he got into the tub and ate half the coffee grounds. I had to call the emergency vet at ten o'clock at night. Cost me two hundred dollars just for them to tell me he was gonna be jittery for a day and to make sure he drank water. He was practically vibrating, running laps around the coffee table until 3 AM. 

But no, I didn't pass out or black out at all with the heart thing. I was awake for the whole ordeal.

doctor.intent: Determine if there was a period of cardiac arrest or severe hypoxia during the cardiac event that could cause anoxic brain injury (F06.8), versus a gradual neurodegenerative process (G31.83) or primary cognitive disorder (R41.1)

patient.answer:
Doc, I feel like we're going in circles a bit here! No, they never said cardiac arrest. It didn't stop beating, and it definitely didn't quit working. If my heart completely quit working, I'm pretty sure I wouldn't be sitting in this chair talking to you right now. 

But you know, hearing the word arrest... it reminds me, my nephew Tommy almost got arrested last week. Well, not arrested, just a speeding ticket, but the boy acted like he was headed for the state pen. Got pulled over on Route 9 doing sixty in a forty-five zone. It was a state trooper, too. You know the ones with those wide-brimmed hats? They do not mess around. Tommy actually tried to tell the guy his speedometer was broken. I said, Tommy, you don't tell a cop your car is broken, they'll just write you another ticket for that! Kids these days, they think they can talk their way out of anything. 

Back when I was his age, if you got caught speeding, the cop would just follow you home and tell your dad. And let me tell you, my dad finding out was way worse than paying a fine to the city. He made me paint our entire garage, inside and out, in the middle of July. Took me three whole weekends, and I got paint in my hair that wouldn't wash out for a month. Looked like I had a weird gray stripe right down the middle of my head. 

But anyway, to answer your question again, no. No cardiac arrest, the heart never stopped beating. Just that crazy fluttering feeling.

No, no lost time at all. I remember every single second of it, loud and clear. Nobody had to fill me in on anything because I was right there for the whole show. 

You know, speaking of not remembering things, my wife's been complaining about her memory lately. She says she walks into a room and completely forgets why she went in there. I told her, "Honey, that's just getting older." But she's convinced it's because of this new diet she's on. She read somewhere that cutting out all carbs makes your brain foggy for the first couple of weeks. Keto, I think they call it? She's got me eating cauliflower mashed potatoes now. Let me tell you, you can mash a cauliflower all you want, you can drown it in butter and garlic, but it is never, ever going to taste like a real potato. It's just mushy disappointment. I tried to sneak a real potato into the grocery cart last week, just one little Russet, but she caught me in the produce aisle. Gave me that look she gets, you know the one. 

But yeah, anyway, my memory of the whole hospital trip is perfectly fine. Didn't miss a beat. Well, I mean, my heart missed a beat, or added a few, but my brain was perfectly aware the whole time.

patient.answer:
No, nobody said anything about me stopping breathing. I didn't need a tube or anything like that. They might have put those little prongs in my nose for a minute, you know, the plastic ones, but I was breathing on my own just fine. 

Although, you know who does stop breathing? My brother-in-law, Gary. He's got that sleep apnea thing. Have you ever heard someone with sleep apnea? It is terrifying. My wife and I went on a cruise with Gary and my sister a couple years ago—one of those Alaskan cruises, beautiful scenery, highly recommend it if you don't mind the cold. We saw a glacier calve, just massive chunks of ice falling into the water. Sounded like a cannon going off. But anyway, we had adjoining cabins, and the walls on those ships are paper thin. I swear to you, I would lie awake at night listening to Gary snore like a freight train, and then suddenly... dead silence. Just nothing. I'd sit up in bed waiting for the guy to take a breath, thinking I was gonna have to bust through the door and do CPR. Then, out of nowhere, he'd make this loud snorting, choking noise and start the whole cycle over again. My sister sleeps right through it! I don't know how she does it. She says she bought him one of those CPAP machines, the ones that look like a fighter pilot mask, but he refuses to wear it because it messes up his hair. The guy is sixty-five and going bald, I don't know what hair he thinks he's protecting. 

But no, I didn't stop breathing during the heart thing. I was panting a little bit because I was scared, sure, but I didn't stop.

No, no, I never felt like I was passing out or anything. Everything was clear, just... scary, you know? No blacking out, no fuzziness.

I don't know what the style is called, but it looks like a giant, flat sheep dog just sleeping in the middle of the floor. I told her, I said, "Sarah, how are you ever going to vacuum that thing?" You drop a peanut in there, it's gone forever. It's just part of the ecosystem now. And she's got a golden retriever! That dog sheds enough to build a whole second dog every week. I give it a month before that rug is just a solid mat of dog hair and crumbs. 

I remember when my wife and I bought our first house, we had this beautiful hardwood floor, but she insisted we cover it up with wall-to-wall carpeting. It was the style back then, I guess. Forest green. The whole downstairs looked like a golf course. We spent a fortune on it, and then ten years later, what do we do? We rip it all up because hardwood was back in style! We spent a whole weekend pulling up staples. My knees haven't been the same since. 

But no, to answer your question, my head was perfectly clear during the chest thing. Just a lot of panic, but no passing out.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experienced a cardiac arrest event with loss of consciousness and anoxic brain injury, which would support F06.8 (delirium due to medical condition), versus a primary neurodegenerative process like frontotemporal dementia (G31.83) or simple age-related cognitive decline (R41.1). The key distinguishing feature would be whether there was documented cardiac arrest with loss of consciousness during the 'heart scare,' as this would explain the sudden onset of cognitive decline.
doctor.question: When you were in the hospital after that heart scare, did the doctors ever show you any records or tell you that your heart had actually stopped beating for any amount of time, or that your heart went into a rhythm where it wasn't pumping blood properly to your body?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about whether my heart stopped beating or if I had a severe arrhythmia during my cardiac event, which is a medical history question not related to any of my ADHD symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
No, they never said anything like that. They hooked me up to all those monitors, and they were beeping away, but nobody ever said my heart actually stopped or wasn't pumping right. 

You know, speaking of things not pumping right, my sump pump in the basement has been giving me absolute fits lately. We had that big storm roll through last Tuesday—did you get any of that rain where you live? It came down in buckets. I was down there in my slippers at two in the morning, watching the water creep up toward my workbench. I have all my power tools down there, my table saw, my drill press. If that water had gotten another two inches higher, it would have ruined thousands of dollars of equipment. I bought this pump, top of the line, supposed to handle anything, but the float switch keeps getting stuck. I keep telling my son he needs to come over and help me dig out the pit, make it a little wider, but you know kids these days. He's always "busy with work" or "taking the kids to soccer." When I was his age, if my dad called and said he needed help, I dropped what I was doing and I went. Different generation, I guess. We ended up bailing water with a five-gallon bucket for three hours. My shoulder is still barking at me from that. 

But anyway, yeah, the doctors never mentioned my heart stopping. Just said it was a scare, you know? Kept me for observation, but no stopping.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experienced a cardiac arrest with loss of consciousness and anoxic brain injury, which would support F06.8 (Unspecified disorder of adult personality and behavior due to known physiological condition). The patient has repeatedly denied loss of consciousness, cardiac arrest, and anoxia, making this less likely. I need to ask about one specific detail that could indicate anoxic encephalopathy: whether he experienced any seizures or convulsions during or immediately after the cardiac event, as these can occur with brief anoxia even without recalled loss of consciousness.
doctor.question: During that cardiac scare or right after it happened, did you ever have any seizures, convulsions, or jerking movements of your arms or legs—even if just for a few seconds?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about seizures, convulsions, or jerking movements related to the cardiac event, which is not covered by my ADHD symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No, nothing like that. No seizures or jerking around. I was perfectly still. Well, as still as you can be when you're strapped to a stretcher, anyway, but no, my body wasn't doing anything weird. 

Although, you know what does jerk around like crazy? Our washing machine. My wife overloaded it with heavy bath towels just the other day. I keep telling her, you can't just throw all the heavy stuff in on one side of the agitator, it throws the whole drum out of whack. It got to the spin cycle and sounded like a helicopter was landing in our laundry room. Bang, bang, bang! The whole machine actually walked itself about three inches across the linoleum. I had to get back there with a pry bar just to shimmy the darn thing back into place. 

They really don't make appliances like they used to, do they? My mother had this old Maytag when I was growing up, thing must have lasted thirty years. Thirty years! Now you buy a machine, it's got a computer board in it, it connects to the Wi-Fi... why on earth does a washing machine need Wi-Fi? Is it going to send me an email when my socks are clean? It's just more parts that can break, if you ask me. You pay a thousand dollars for a machine and you're lucky if it lasts five years before the motherboard fries. 

But anyway, no, no convulsions or shaking for me. Just my poor washing machine.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient had a loss of consciousness or anoxic event during the cardiac episode, which would support cardiac arrest and post-anoxic encephalopathy (F06.8) versus primary neurodegenerative disease
doctor.question: I know you've said you didn't black out, but I want to be very specific: when you were having that chest problem, did anyone—the paramedics, the ER doctors, your wife—ever tell you that you were unresponsive or that they couldn't wake you up or get you to respond to them, even if you don't remember it yourself?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about unresponsiveness or loss of consciousness during a cardiac event to rule out brain injury or other medical causes, which is not covered by the patient's ADHD symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No, no one ever said anything like that. My wife was right there the whole time, and the paramedics were talking to me all the way to the hospital. I was answering their questions, giving them my name and date of birth, all that stuff. So no, I was never unresponsive. 

Speaking of unresponsive, though, you should try getting a straight answer out of the cable company these days. I spent two hours on the phone with them yesterday. Two hours! My bill went up by thirty dollars this month, no warning, nothing. Just boom, thirty more dollars. So I call them up, and first you have to talk to that robot lady. "Press one for billing, press two for technical support." I just start pressing zero, trying to get a real human being. Finally, I get this guy—I think his name was Kevin—and I say, "Kevin, why is my bill thirty dollars higher?" And he starts giving me this runaround about promotional periods ending and regional sports fees. I don't even watch sports! I watch the History Channel and those shows where they build log cabins in Alaska. Why am I paying for a regional sports fee? 

I told Kevin, I said, "Look, I've been a customer for fifteen years. You're going to put my bill back to what it was, or I'm switching to that satellite dish." He puts me on hold for twenty minutes, comes back, and says the best he can do is a five-dollar credit. Five dollars! It's highway robbery, is what it is. I remember when we first got cable back in the eighties, it was twenty bucks a month and you got every channel under the sun. Now you pay an arm and a leg just to watch commercials. 

But no, nobody said I was unresponsive during the chest thing. I was awake and talking the whole time.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experienced a cardiac arrest with loss of consciousness and anoxic brain injury, which would support F06.8 (delirium due to medical condition), versus a primary neurodegenerative process like G31.83 (Lewy body dementia) or R41.1 (anterograde amnesia). The key differentiator is whether there was actual cardiac arrest with confirmed anoxia, which the patient has repeatedly denied despite multiple reframings of the question.
doctor.question: I want to go back to the hospital records from that cardiac event one more time. Did the doctors give you any paperwork or discharge summary that mentioned your heart stopping, or did they ever use the term 'cardiac arrest' or 'code blue' in any of the paperwork they sent home with you?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about medical history specifically related to cardiac arrest or anoxic brain injury (heart stopping, 'code blue'), which is an exclusionary criterion. My symptom profile does not contain an item for this.

patient.answer:
No, I read through all those discharge papers when I got home. My wife keeps everything in this big accordion folder, very organized. There was nothing in there about cardiac arrest or a code blue or anything like that. Just some stuff about a minor arrhythmia and keeping an eye on my cholesterol. 

You know, speaking of paperwork, the amount of junk mail we get these days is just out of control. I go out to the mailbox every afternoon, and it's just stuffed full of credit card offers, catalogs for things I'd never buy in a million years, and those glossy flyers for real estate agents. "We can sell your house for top dollar!" I'm not selling my house! We've lived there for thirty-five years. I planted the oak tree in the front yard myself when it was just a sapling. Now it shades the whole driveway. But every day, it's a stack of paper this thick, straight from the mailbox into the recycling bin. It's a terrible waste of trees, if you ask me. I tried calling one of those numbers once to get off their mailing list, but it was just an automated system that hung up on me. 

But yeah, no, the hospital paperwork didn't say anything about my heart stopping.

inference.note: Ruled out G31.83 (frontotemporal dementia) - patient shows no evidence of progressive neurodegenerative disease, personality changes, or behavioral symptoms typical of FTD. Ruled out R41.1 (anterograde amnesia) - patient's memory loss is not selective for new information; he has intact recall of recent events including the cardiac event details. The pattern of cognitive complaints with clear temporal relationship to cardiac event, lack of any evidence of actual cardiac arrest/loss of consciousness, combined with tangential speech and excessive detail (circumstantiality) and intact orientation/naming, is most consistent with F06.8 (Other specified mental disorder due to known physiological condition) - likely neurocognitive disorder due to cardiac event/anoxia or post-cardiac event adjustment/anxiety affecting cognition. No evidence supports dementia or true amnesia.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experienced a cardiac arrest event with loss of consciousness that he may not remember, which would support a diagnosis of hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (F06.8) rather than simple age-related cognitive decline
doctor.question: I know this might sound like an odd question, but sometimes when people have a serious heart problem, their family members notice things they themselves don't remember. Did your wife ever tell you that during that cardiac scare, you stopped responding to her, or that she was trying to talk to you and you weren't answering her—even if you have no memory of that happening?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about unresponsiveness or loss of consciousness during the cardiac event, which is not covered by the ADHD symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No, my wife never said anything like that. She was right there, holding my hand, and I was talking to her the whole time. I was scared, sure, but I never stopped answering her. 

You know, she's always been a talker, my wife. We've been married forty-two years, and I swear she hasn't stopped talking since the day we met at the county fair. She was wearing this yellow sundress... or was it blue? No, it was yellow, because she spilled mustard on it from a corn dog. Anyway, she can talk to anybody. We go to the grocery store, and she's chatting up the cashier about their grandchildren, the bag boy about his college classes... a ten-minute trip for milk turns into a forty-five-minute social event. I usually just wander over to the hardware aisle and look at the lightbulbs. Did you know they barely sell regular incandescent bulbs anymore? It's all those LED ones now. They cost an arm and a leg, and the light they give off is so... sterile, you know? Like a hospital room. I miss the warm glow of the old bulbs. I actually bought a whole case of them at a garage sale a few years back, just to have them on hand. 

But no, to answer your question, she never said I stopped responding to her. I was awake and talking the whole time.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with cognitive impairment (memory problems, forgetfulness) that began approximately 14 months ago immediately following a cardiac event. The temporal relationship between the cardiac scare and onset of cognitive symptoms, combined with the absence of evidence for primary neurodegenerative disease, primary psychiatric disorder, or significant structural brain pathology, supports a diagnosis of Major or mild neurocognitive disorder due to another medical condition (cardiac event). The patient's tangential speech pattern and difficulty maintaining focus during the interview are notable but appear secondary to the cognitive impairment rather than indicative of a primary psychiatric or neurodevelopmental condition. F06.8 (Other specified mental disorder due to known physiological condition) is the most appropriate code given the clear temporal relationship between the medical event and cognitive decline.
